title: Computational Work Extraction: The Complexity of Catalysts
authors: Atul Singh Arora, Shantanav Chakraborty, Alexandru Cojocaru, Sreyas Saminathan, Uttam Singh
abstract: We prove maximal separations: $n$-qubit systems can have $Θ(n)$ ergotropy, while every efficient process extracts negligible work, even for Hamiltonians consisting of single-qubit terms. We establish an unconditional existential separation and give an explicit construction in the random oracle model. Assuming the existence of quantum-secure pseudorandom functions, this separation extends to the plain model.   This work uncovers an important connection between ergotropy and the complexity of catalytic computation---computation where auxiliary qubits must be finally restored to their initial state. Relative to a random oracle, we establish relational and decision problems that: (i) can be solved efficiently with $λ$ catalysts; but (ii) cannot be solved by any algorithm with $cλ$ catalysts, for any $c<1$. We show this by proving query lower bounds for quantum-space bounded algorithms.   As a consequence, for computational ergotropy, catalysts prove to be surprisingly powerful---there is a family of Hamiltonians and states for which catalysts enable efficient extraction of the full $Θ(n)$ ergotropy, while every efficient non-catalytic process extracts negligible work. Furthermore, catalysts also allow us to introduce and instantiate the notion of pseudoergotropy---analogous to pseudorandomness. On the other hand, we show catalysts do not change (information-theoretic) ergotropy.   Finally, our work also sheds light on the classical aspect of the problem. First, most of our constructions rely on classical states and Hamiltonians and therefore imply analogous results for classical ergotropy. Second, we show that certain proof of quantumness protocols can be used to generically separate classical and quantum catalytic ergotropy.
summary: This work rigorously analyzes the relationship between theoretical work extractability (ergotropy) and what can be achieved by efficient quantum computation. It proves that the introduction of catalytic resources dramatically enhances the extractable work in the computational setting, leading to significant separations from non-catalytic processes. This has implications for understanding the fundamental limits of energy harvesting in quantum information processing.
main_problem: The paper investigates the gap between the theoretically maximal work extractable from a quantum system (ergotropy) and the work extractable by computationally efficient processes, especially when auxiliary qubits (catalysts) are involved.
main_result: Catalysts are shown to be surprisingly powerful for computational work extraction, enabling the extraction of the full $\Theta(n)$ ergotropy in certain cases where non-catalytic processes extract negligible work. Furthermore, explicit separations are established between computational and catalytic capabilities.
method: The analysis uses rigorous theoretical tools, including establishing query lower bounds, employing random oracle models, and constructing explicit state/Hamiltonian families to prove computational separations.
model_or_system: The system is an isolated quantum system described by a state $ho$ on an $n$-qubit Hilbert space, evolving under a Hamiltonian $H$. The processes are constrained by computational efficiency (polynomial-sized circuits) and the use of catalytic resources.
key_observables: Ergotropy ($	ext{erg}_ho, H$), Computational Ergotropy ($	ext{c}	ext{erg}$), and the catalytic work-potential.
important_parameters: The system size $n$, the number of catalysts $\lambda$, and the constant $c$ used in the separation bounds ($c<1$).
main_assumptions: The results are established unconditionally in the random oracle model, and the analysis often relies on asymptotic settings involving families of states and Hamiltonians.
figures_summary: Not specified, but the notes refer to a conceptual comparison (Figure 1) contrasting information-theoretic vs. computational work extraction under different catalyst restoration requirements.
paper_structure: The paper progresses by defining the key concepts (ergotropy vs. computational ergotropy), establishing the separation using random oracle models, demonstrating the power of catalysts via problem-solving separations, and concluding with analogies to classical systems.
why_interesting: It provides a deep theoretical understanding of the physical limitations of energy extraction in quantum computation, showing that computational constraints can drastically alter the perceived thermodynamic potential of a quantum state.
